# CC06: 海岳开襟 Haiyue Kaijin

Wave 3 · Changchun Yuan · 3D: `/reconstruction/3d.html?b=CC06` · Page: `/scenes/#CC06` · Row: `research/buildings/CC06-haiyue-kaijin/`

## What it was

海岳开襟 Haiyue Kaijin, "Open Breast to Sea and Mountain", was a three-storey building on a round raised base in the pool north of 思永斋, with an arch on each of the four sides (S05 j83:11a: 中有圓式崇基其上樓宇三層為海嶽開襟四旁枋楔各一; E0145). Finished 1747 (E0164, S991). Plaques: 海岳开襟 inside the lower storey, 青瑶屿 on the south eave, 乘六龙 on the top storey (S05 j83:11a); the park adds 得沧洲趣 for the middle storey (S991). The park's text gives the main tower five bays a side below with double-eaved porches and three bays a side on the two upper storeys, double-eaved halls north and south, four double-eaved square pavilions, 36 bays of curved gallery and four arches, on an island with stone revetment, white marble balustrade, a landing on each side and 24 lacebark pines (S991; Malone's round terraced island with four flights of steps, E0163). The island was about 90 m across (E0164, E0165). It survived the burning of 1860 in mid-lake, was visited by Guangxu and Cixi, and was taken apart in 1900 (S991; E0164, E0451).

From the inventory row: **built** by 1759 poem [j83:11a-b]; 1747; **destroyed** 1860; on the 1873 survival list (S06); survived 1860; later loss; survived 1860; lost around 1900 (S05, S02, S06, S01, S337, S361).

## The scene itself

### The leaf of 1744, its poem and preface

Not one of the Forty Scenes of 1744.

### How later sources differ

The group was cut down under Jiaqing and Daoguang (S991, no date or document given); repairs of 1778 and 1791 are recorded (E0165). A photograph of about 1882 by the Comte de Semallé shows the main hall then as a single-storey hall with a single-eaved pyramidal roof (S991): so the three-storey tower of S05 may not have stood in 1860. Under Guangxu a long timber bridge was added on the west shore (S991). Jiaqing still climbed 'the tower' in 1797 and 1816 (E0162, E0152).

## What survives today

Taken apart in 1900 by Banner looters after months of resistance by the eunuch guards, and its trees felled; troops dug pits for treasure in the 1920s (S991). The round island was cleared of rubble in 1993 and its stone revetment re-laid; lotus ponds surround it today (S991). A totem park stood on it 1995-2007 (E0165). Ruin photographs P0413, P0414, P0503.

No excavation or survey of its remains found in this round.
